utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There are a few matters to deal with before we hear the witness's evidence. The Chamber will now first issue an oral ruling in relation to the accused's notice of 15th of May, 2012, that he intends to call Dr. Derek Allsop as an expert in his defence case. Allsop is currently listed as the fifth witness this week. On the 17th of May, 2012, the Prosecution filed a response to the accused's notice, wherein it does not contest the relevance of the subject matter of the report but states that it does not accept its conclusions, requests the opportunity to cross-examine Allsop, and to make submissions as to the admissibility of the report and asks that the Chamber defer its findings with respect to Allsop's expertise and the admissibility of the report until after he appears for testimony. As has been the practice of the Chamber throughout this case, a decision as to the admission of the report which is challenged by the Prosecution will only be made after Allsop's testimony. However, with respect to the challenge to Allsop's expertise, the Chamber considers that it is in the interests of justice to rule on it before his testimony as there would be no reason to call Allsop should the Chamber consider he did not qualify as an expert witness. In this regard, the Chamber notes the Prosecution's submissions in the response that it is yet unclear whether Dr. Allsop has the special knowledge, specific experience, or skills needed to assist the Trial Chamber in assessing "whether it was possible to calculate the distance that the mortar shell travelled before exploding at the Markale Market on the 5th of February, 1994, as claimed by Berko Zecevic." The Chamber has conducted its own assessment of Allsop's CV which shows that he is a mechanical engineer with 24 years of academic and research experience in relation to weapons testing, ammunition, and ballistics. While the Chamber agrees with the Prosecution that Allsop's CV lacks some detail and that it contains no reference to his expertise in the area of 120-millimetre mortar projectiles used in BiH during the conflict, the Chamber nevertheless considers that his qualifications and experience are such that he has sufficient expertise to testify in these proceedings pursuant to Rule 94 bis in relation to the possibility of calculating the distance travelled by the mortar shell before exploding at Markale Market on the 5th of February, 1994. In addition, during its cross-examination, the Prosecution will have the opportunity to inquire with Allsop as to his expertise with regards to 120-millimetre mortars, which will go to the overall weight the Chamber will attribute to the findings in his report. The Chamber hereby decides that Allsop shall testify as an expert pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules. For a couple of next matters, the Chamber will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more matter, Mr. Robinson, in open session. The Chamber has noticed that for the first three witnesses scheduled for this week, Joudry, Russell, and Gauthier, you have included in their respective Rule 92 ter notifications a request that a representative of their government be present during their testimony. In light of what I just mentioned in private session and the fact that the Chamber sees no difference between this condition and other conditions under Rule 70 which need to be properly addressed to the Chamber, can you tell us where the request for a representative of the Canadian government originated from, which is the legal basis for such a request, and if indeed there is a Canadian governmental representative present today waiting for the permission of the Chamber to enter the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The request for the representative to be present came from the Government of Canada in our discussions with -- for this witness, but they have decided not to ask to be present so there's no one here for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That resolves everything. Unless there's any other matter to raise, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D25487 in e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, have you had a look at a hard copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you signed this copy; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I did, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement an accurate reflection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I put the same questions to you here today, would your answers to those questions be identical to the answers provided in your statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you're not tendering any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Tieger? Yes, that will be admitted as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to read out a very brief summary of your summary in English. [In English] Steven Joudry is a retired colonel of the Canadian Armed Forces. He was a trained artillery officer within the Royal Canadian Artillery. Part of his training was in field techniques for crater analysis. He later taught field crater analysis to other army personnel within the Canadian Armed Forces. He either conducted or was involved in about a hundred crater analyses during his career. In May 1993, Colonel Joudry was deployed to the former Yugoslavia as a senior staff officer in operations and plans at the United Nations Protection Forces headquarters in Zagreb, Croatia. He remained there until March 1994. While at UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, Colonel Joudry became aware of an explosion at the Markale Market-place in Sarajevo on 5th of February, 1994. He was not part of the team which investigated that explosion; however, after the crater analysis report by the UN investigation team, he was asked to review their report. Colonel Joudry had serious reservations about the procedure used for crater analysis in the market-place explosion and how the results were being used. To begin with, field crater analysis is not accurate enough to determine culpability, even under ideal conditions. The fact that much of the information in this case was gathered hours or even days after the explosion, rather than from a hot undisturbed crater, in a public area, in his opinion, rendered many of the results questionable. In other field situations, such an analysis would have been discarded. Colonel Joudry noted that the angle of descent of the 120-millimetre mortar that landed on the Markale Market could not be reliably measured because the first UN team had reportedly removed the tail fin and disturbed the crater without measuring the angle of descent. Once they had done that, it was highly likely the fuse tunnel was disturbed and, therefore, it was no longer possible to calculate the angle of descent with any degree of accuracy. Without knowing the angle of descent, it was impossible to accurately calculate the possible charges used and therefore the possible range in distance, minimum and maximum, that the projectile could have travelled. From his detailed review of the material and using his knowledge and experience in gunnery and field operations, Colonel Joudry reached the following conclusions: First, he noted the limitations of field crater analysis and the unreliable nature of the conclusions as a basis to assign culpability, particularly in the theatre of operations, former Yugoslavia, where it was widely believed that all sides in the conflict had used various forms of deception of tactical information for strategic or political purposes. However, using the data as obtained from the analyses conducted by the UN military teams following the explosion, he completed the steps of a normal full field crater analysis. This included the assumption that the weapon was a 120-millimetre mortar and using the estimated data on the angle of impact which he then used to assess the likely charge increments. He concluded that using the flawed data, one conclusion could have been that the projectile was fired from an area which slightly straddled the confrontation line north-east of Sarajevo, but 95 per cent of which was on the Bosnian government side in the known confrontation line at the time. Colonel Joudry also opined that if the aim of the culpable party was to have the explosion occur in the market-place that day and appear like a mortar round fired from a distance, the most accurate way to have achieved that was to launch the projectile by hand from the nearby roof. Given the relatively small size of the market-place as an indirect fire target and that the area had not been subjected to intense targeting hours or even days prior to the explosion, for a single mortar round to have been fired at the market-place to hit it would have been virtually impossible. [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't have any further questions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Joudry, as you have noted, your evidence was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and you will be now cross-examined by the Prosecution team. Yes, is it you, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President. Thank you. And good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. First I have a couple of preliminary questions. With regard to the crater analyses that you were involved in that he referred to, were those primarily or exclusively training exercises?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Primarily training exercises, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And were -- did those involve shells or projectiles fired into fields or did they involve projectiles fired onto asphalt or the streets of cities?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Primarily it would have been in fields; however, there were many instances where the projectiles would have landed on hard surfaces, in some cases asphalt, in some cases roads, but none of them would have been in inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the pattern left by a shell or a mortar projectile is decidedly different if it lands on a soft surface than if it lands on a hard surface?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the majority of analyses in which you were involved involved artillery rather than -- or howitzers and guns rather than mortars?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Certainly on balance the -- most of them would have been artillery, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that none of them, to the best of your recollection, involved 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the examination that you undertook from Zagreb and the conclusions you reached, is it correct that those were not part of any official UN investigation?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct. I think it's important to note that what I did was a review of the previous analyses with limited information that I had available, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that limited information was, I presume, the materials that had been or certainly some of the materials that had been produced by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct. Probably the only additional information that I used in my review that they didn't, at least to the best of my knowledge, was I do recall seeing a couple of photographs after the incident and I do recall perusing the operations logs of the UNPROFOR headquarters operations centre around that particular period of time. And I don't recall if the actual review done by UNPROFOR on the analysis actually included that, but other than that it was limited to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that you did not see any photographs that were produced by UNPROFOR, but you did see a couple of photographs that you understood had -- were not available to UNPROFOR? Perhaps I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I don't recall where the photographs came from. I just recall they were part of the package that I was -- that I had access to. And in the review I don't recall seeing those photographs being referred to in the actual analyses because, of course, the analyses would have been on the ground. I didn't have -- I never actually saw the crater myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You didn't speak to any of those officials who actually participated in the formal investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: As much as I would have liked to, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You didn't prepare or at least you don't recall having prepared a written report of your assessment and conclusions?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Given that my job was a staff officer, I'm almost certain I would have, but I don't recall that specifically. I do recall, however, providing an oral briefing to a group of officials based on my results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you don't recall specifically who those officials were?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, I don't. I believe, I'm not certain, but I believe it was a regular scheduled operations meeting and I happened to be one of the agenda items on that particular day to brief the military personnel on the results of my review.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, although you've alluded to it, you did not examine or even see the crater; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not examine or even go to the scene; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not examine or even see the tail fin or stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, I saw pictures of it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. You didn't examine any physical evidence?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we noted before, you didn't interview any witnesses?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, nevertheless, as noted in the summary of your statement, you reached certain conclusions, and among those conclusions were the -- or was the expression of serious reservations about the procedures and how they were being used and certain views about what was done or not done. I want to look at some of those, Mr. Joudry. Now, in the summary, Mr. Karadzic referred to your concern that much of the information was gathered hours or even days after the explosion rather than from a hot, undisturbed crater, and that that was -- that information was gathered hours or even days after the explosion in a public area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Joudry, do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it's on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have one in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there's one available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that would be helpful, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, that's always a helpful suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Joudry, I was just referring to paragraph 16 at page 3. I'll give you a moment to orient yourself with the --

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: All right. I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it seems that throughout your statement you continued to emphasize the -- what you saw as a matter of concern, that is, the alleged delay in the arrival of UNPROFOR and the gathering of information. So at paragraph 26 you again refer to the delay in UN teams arriving at the scene as one of the factors that led you to conclude that the explosion was caused by or possibly or likely or -- to have been caused by a hand-thrown projectile. So, Colonel, how long was it in your view before UNPROFOR officials came to the scene?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I had access to the written material at the time. It was my understanding that although the first teams had perhaps arrived on the scene within -- within ten minutes the actual -- the first crater analysis time that I saw was about two hours after the actual explosion. And there would have been a lot of information that would have been important, in my view, as a teacher of crater analysis that would have been gained in those first few minutes. And I -- there was no information in those reports that information was gathered during those critical moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, the emphasis in your report appears to be the delay in the arrival of UNPROFOR, and I presume that that's, at least in large part, a concern about the destruction of evidence, the deterioration of evidence, the contamination of evidence, and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, but keeping in mind that this type of field crater analysis really, in my view, was inappropriate to use it in the context of a forensic science, but clearly some elements of that would have been appropriate. So for the evidence or the information to have been obtained, I believe several of the analyses of the crater were done several hours after the explosion. And that information, while useful, certainly would be questionable if you were trying to assign without doubt culpability, which is what my concern was. The UN was using crater analysis inappropriately in this case given the circumstances around that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Joudry, I understand your military background and we've already alluded to your experience in gunnery, but I do not understand that you have any experience in forensic analysis or judicial proceedings; that would be correct, right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I also noted that in a couple of places in your statement you try to assess the -- or you purport to assess the utility or effect of the information that is made available from the observations at the scene or crater analysis on any ultimate determination of responsibility. So my suggestion would be that we leave that to the Judges and we simply focus for the moment on what was done and what factors they -- that -- the conclusions that were reached relied upon. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So first of all, with respect to the -- any concern about destruction of evidence, deterioration of evidence, it is correct - is it not? - that there was essentially a continuous UN presence on the scene, with two extremely brief exceptions, from about five minutes after the explosion until after the time that French Battalion analysts arrived and removed the stabiliser from the crater; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I have no specific knowledge of that. As I said, I've just reviewed the material that was presented to me. I cannot confirm or deny anything with respect to who had control over the scene at the time, and I wasn't so much looking at it from an evidence perspective. I was looking at it from tactical and field information. Not so much evidence. As you have indicated, that's not my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest, Mr. Joudry, that you did have specific knowledge of it because that is contained in the UNPROFOR report. So at --

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, all I'm saying, sir, is I can't confirm whether it's true or not. It's just that that -- you already have that information. I had the same information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That there was a continuous UN presence on the scene, and it's further true that the FrenchBat crater analysis team arrived and confirmed that the crater appeared to be fully intact and fresh. When they arrived at the scene it did not appear to have been tampered with. That's also contained in the UNPROFOR report; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's what I recall reading, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And since you were never at the scene, you have, I presume, no basis for disputing the observations of those who were directly at the scene and seeing it firsthand?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, another aspect of your expressed concern was the removal of the tail fin or stabiliser from its position in the crater where it had been -- it was embedded deep in the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we noted from the summary that was read, you went on to observe - and that's at paragraph 23 of your statement, just to orient you - your concern about the likelihood that the -- what you call the fuse tunnel, and that means the tunnel created by the stabiliser in this case, was disturbed and therefore it would be no longer possible to calculate the angle of descent with any degree of accuracy. That was your concern and that's what you put in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: The fuse tunnel in a crater isn't caused by the stabiliser; it's caused by the fuse that goes into the ground and it creates an opening. And in this case in the mortar crater, the stabiliser would have gone in behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the fuse in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You don't. So you don't know whether the fuse went in or the fuse was destroyed on impact? You don't have any idea one way or the other. What we do know -- that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What we do know is that the stabiliser went in the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And so when I refer to the tunnel now, I'm going to be referring to that hole, all right, for clarity.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that hole or tunnel where the stabiliser was embedded, do you know its size; that is, how deep the stabiliser went in and the extent of the hole created?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: My recollection from reading the reports was that the fuse tunnel itself was in the order of 10 to 15 centimetres in the ground and it's -- and the stabiliser was -- was in the fuse tunnel to some degree there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the UNPROFOR report will speak for itself. My recollection is it was about 8 to 10 centimetres below the surface and about 20 to 30 centimetres in total deep, but as I say the record will speak for itself on that one. Now, when that happens, I imagine -- and the stabiliser is subsequently removed from its position in the ground. It's presumably fair to say that one of a few possibilities exist. Now, one is that when it's removed the ground will crumble around it and it will eliminate the tunnel that was originally created. Another one -- another possibility is that the cavity or tunnel created by the stabiliser would be expanded by the effort to remove it. And a third possibility, presumably, is that it was removed from the tunnel or hole with minimal disturbance, something like a cork from a bottle. Would you agree with those three possibilities or is there one you would add or omit?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, that sounds reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you did not examine the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't -- you didn't have a chance to see for yourself the extent to which any disturbance occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But those on the scene did; is that right? Are you aware, Mr. Joudry, that one of those persons at the scene who saw the tunnel testified before this Court and indeed before a previous Court?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That doesn't surprise me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware, in fact, that the tunnel - as he observed it - was intact?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, that's one of the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not a possibility. It's what the person who was at the scene looking at the tunnel said .

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger can't be testifying here. And first of all, I'm wondering if --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not testifying Colonel Hamill is testifying at transcript page 9729.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the correct way to put the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that transcript page Colonel Hamill said that it was -- that an accurate reading could be taken when he did so because the fuse tunnel was still -- in effect still intact. That's information you didn't have access to; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yeah, that -- I hadn't heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Except that that's exactly what Colonel Hamill said in his report, because he did take readings of the -- for the -- both the bearing and the angle of descent, and that's contained in his report. So did you forget that?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, that was -- I recall -- I don't recall the individual you're speaking of, but I certainly recall that being part of the information that I had at my disposal. But as I said, I was -- not having seen the crater myself, and I was a teacher of crater analysis, not the observer of the particular crater in this case, and that there's a principle involved and that is: You don't disturb the crater. And once you remove a piece of evidence such as you've just described, you've basically -- regardless of what was left of the fuse tunnel, you now have a disturbed crater and all your information after that is questionable. That was my point to UNPROFOR at the time. And this information, by the way, would have been gathered by the people conducting the analysis who should have, if they were the first ones on the scene, if they were trained in crater analysis, I find it absolutely incredible that they would have removed the tail fin before gathering the rest of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So what you told the UNPROFOR officials was that as a matter of principle it's not a good idea and one shouldn't remove the stabiliser before one takes measurements, that -- that's right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that although you hadn't seen the tunnel that remained and although you weren't aware of the extent to which, if any, the tunnel was actually physically disturbed, you were simply concerned about this violation of principle and wanted to register it as a possible source of concern?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the analysis undertaken by Colonel Hamill using the stabiliser -- tunnel created by the stabiliser, are you aware of the fact that there was another UNPROFOR official who also did an analysis of the angle of descent based on the fuse tunnel -- excuse me, the stabiliser tunnel?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, from what I recall there were in excess of seven or eight different analyses done on the crater, as I said, from a couple of hours to several days after the incident. So yes, there would have been a number of people taking or gathering information from that crater. But I -- notwithstanding the fact that the expertise, if you want to call it that, that I had in this area is approaching 20 years, 20 years ago, unless I'm mistaken when we speak of the fuse tunnel, the fuse tunnel is not created by the stabiliser in a mortar crater. It was one of the inconsistencies that I saw in the information. In a projectile, if you have a crater that is as deep as this one apparently was, clearly the fuse went into the ground and impacted sometime between when it hit the ground and when it penetrated the surface. So the fuse of the projectile, the pointy end of the projectile, would have created this tunnel, and then the stabiliser would have gone in behind it. That's how it's created.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't want to replicate unnecessarily a ground we've already covered, Mr. Joudry, but I thought we addressed that earlier, and that is I had asked you what you knew about the fuse itself and whether it had been destroyed or whether it had created a tunnel on its own. And then we agreed, I thought, that the one thing we did know -- or that you did know, rather, was that the stabiliser was in the ground occupying a hole or a tunnel in the ground and that's what was removed and that's what we've been talking about in terms of cavity, hole, or tunnel that was

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just concerned that the Court would understand that the hole is not created by the stabiliser. The hole is created by the fuse itself of the projectile, which explosion is no longer there. So I just -- it may be a moot point, but I just wanted to make sure that I was correcting that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, if the -- well, let's leave that for the moment because, as I said, I don't want to go over the same ground. Irrespective of the distinction you're drawing here, the fact is - we can agree, I think - that it was the stabiliser that was occupying that hole that we're talking about, hole, cavity, or tunnel that we're talking about, and it was the stabiliser that was removed and it was that hole, cavity, or tunnel that was subsequently used by UNPROFOR officials to calculate the angle of descent and the bearing. All correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right. I guess the point I'm trying to clarify, though, that if there wasn't -- if the projectile had not penetrated the ground and exploded, there wouldn't be a fuse tunnel, and therefore you would have found -- possibly in this case you would have found the stabiliser in and around the crater but you might not have found it in the hole because there wouldn't have been a hole. I guess that's what I'm trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, we'll talk about that in a moment in any event, but there is by the way a technique known as the fuse tunnel technique for calculating, among other things, the angle of descent of the projectile; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And that's basically using the angle of that hole to make the determination of the angle at which the projectile impacted on the ground?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And whether -- and that term "fuse tunnel" or the technique is a term of art and was used in -- by the UNPROFOR officials here, for example, in describing the method they used when they examined this cavity we've been discussing for some moments now?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the conclusion reached by Colonel Hamill when he calculated the angle of descent using that tunnel, and do you recall the conclusion reached by any other UNPROFOR official in undertaking the same analysis?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Not specifically, but as I said I remember reading the analyses conducted by at least seven or eight different individuals. I don't recall Colonel Hamill's data specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. We better give some time for the translators to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Mr. Joudry, that's a reference to the fact, sometimes forgotten by even the participants who are here every day, that you're being translated and therefore if questions and answers proceed too quickly there's no time for the translation. So I will endeavour to remember that and I alert you to the same concern.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Thank you for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: So I take it you would not disagree then that the angle of descent determined by Colonel Hamill was a 900 -- between 950 and 1100 mils which would be -- which would calculate to 53.5 to 61.9 degrees?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That sounds about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And that another UNPROFOR official found an approximate angle of descent after looking at and utilising the cavity or tunnel of approximately 1.000 to 1100 mils, and that would be -- that would translate to 56.2 to 61.9 degrees; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: If that was the information in the analyses that I would have seen, then obviously yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. So those two UNPROFOR officials on the scene looking at the intact crater as Colonel Hamill described it and using the fuse tunnel and/or any other techniques they deemed appropriate found consistent assessments of the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I never had any dispute with the information that was gathered at the scene, the calculations that were made. My concern that I expressed to the UNPROFOR officials was in the manner in which that information had been gained, the nature and scope of the crater analysis, and the conclusions that UNPROFOR officials were making with regards to the information.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Incidentally I alluded earlier to the various possibilities of impact on the tunnel when the stabiliser was removed. Can you think of any good way of testing the impact of removing the stabiliser on that tunnel? For example, would it be useful to determine the effect, if any, on the removal of the stabiliser from the tunnel to re-insert the stabiliser and see whether it fell in because the hole had been enlarged or whether it couldn't go in because the hole had been filled or whether it fit snugly like a silver slipper on Cinderella's foot?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, without seeing the crater and the actual soil conditions, I can't say, but certainly anybody who would have made that decision to re-insert the stabiliser into the tunnel would have made that assessment. And by the way, I should add that there is a method in crater analysis that in the case of where you don't have a stabiliser there to remove but you actually have a defined fuse tunnel, one of the methods is actually to take a piece of wood or a stick and insert it into the fuse tunnel and measure it that way. So the re-insertion of the stabiliser, if it was the decision of somebody on the ground doing the crater analysis, that is a reasonable way to come up with an estimate. But once again, it's an estimate and if you're basing a lot of information on that - which is what they were in this case - I just wanted to make sure that the UNPROFOR officials were aware that the level of accuracy they were deal with here was very wide.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, in fact the extent to which it's -- I accept your position as you stated that your concern was that UNPROFOR officials be aware of the potential impact of the removal of the stabiliser. But the reality is that its impact on the level of accuracy would vary depending on the nature of that removal, the nature of the soil, any subsequent testing to see the extent to which the stabiliser fit well or didn't, and that's -- and those factors would be the determining ones in whether or not the level of accuracy was very wide or reasonably narrow; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: The military officials on the ground who conducted that first crater analysis and decided to re-insert the tail fin basically did what I just described, which is, they acted as if it was simply a fuse tunnel there and re-inserted an object in there to take an angle, which is acceptable in crater analysis procedures. You accept the fact that what you're doing is you're getting an estimate of the angle of impact and it's -- it's -- in this case or in most cases it's not -- you know, the degree of accuracy is impossible to determine, really.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, let me be clear on that. I didn't say that the UNPROFOR officials re-inserted the tail fin. I don't know exactly where -- if you believe that you read that somewhere in the UNPROFOR report or not. I'm talking about other officials.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, the folks who were on the ground who had done some of the crater analysis, my understanding is they had re-inserted the tail fin into the fuse tunnel to in part get this angle of impact, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Bosnian forensic officials re-inserted the tail fin?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the tail fin was in possession of the Bosnian government officials after its removal by FreBat IV crater analysis and until it was re-examined by UNPROFOR officials sometime later?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I remember reading that in the reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber has received evidence, Mr. Joudry, and that can be found for example at P2317 at page 5, regarding the study of the circumstances of the Markale incident by a technical commission from Bosnian authorities, in which they recount the re-insertion of the stabiliser, the reconstruction of the position of the stabiliser, and took a reading from that position. So do you know whether you were aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I don't recall that specifically, but I do remember part of the information I had was that some of the analysis of the angle of fall involved a re-insertion of the tail fin into the crater.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And this Court has also heard evidence from the technician or the technical official who was involved in that who explained to the Court that the stabiliser fit snugly back into the position and allowed him to be confident that it was back in the position it had been in at the time -- before it had been removed?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: If that was his evidence, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact, Mr. Joudry, that the calculations of the angle of descent resulting from that reconstruction were essentially the same as those undertaken by Colonel Hamill and by the other UNPROFOR analysis that I referred to, that is, in the range of 55- to 65 degrees, basically roughly 60 degrees?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That sounds reasonable, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Mr. Joudry, I want to look next at your assessment that using the firing tables you were able to determine a minimum or a maximum range -- and by the way, I'm now referring to paragraph 24(B) of your report. And what I want to discuss with you is the portion of your statement - I referred to it earlier as a "report," it's a statement of course - that was contained in the summary by Mr. Karadzic to the effect that the minimum and maximum range of the projectile was likely fired from an area which slightly straddled the confrontation line but 95 per cent of which was on the Bosnian government side of the confrontation line. So that's what I want to speak to you about now.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, in reaching that, the conclusion or the opinion expressed in 24(B), to assert that the projectile was likely fired from or more likely to have been fired from Bosnian-controlled territory, you used the angle of descent arrived at by the UNPROFOR officials that we talked about a few moments ago; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: From my recollection, I used the ranges within which those angles had been measured, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And then you applied them against the firing tables for the appropriate weaponry?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's what I would have done, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first of all, you said at 24(B) using the data obtained by the UN military teams you "completed the steps of a normal full field crater analysis." That's what you stated in your amalgamated -- it your witness statement; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to be clear, that would be a normal full field crater analysis with the exception of the fact that you didn't go to the scene, you didn't examine the crater, you didn't examine the tail fin, you didn't examine any physical evidence, and you didn't interview witnesses?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, I -- by "full crater analysis" I mean take -- I was concerned, and I explained this to the UNPROFOR officials, that the analysis that they had reviewed or the analysis that they had had missed one step, so I basically completed that final step which would have been done in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And you consider that step to be the application of the angle of descent to the data available in the firing tables for a 120-millimetre mortar to determine the various distances between firing location and impact of the projectile based on the number of charges?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that was the -- at the time that was the contemporary approach to one of the final steps in crater analysis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, noting the time, I'll probably get caught in the middle of a question and answer if I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, how much longer would you need, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Estimating about an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Mr. Joudry, you indicated just before we adjourned that you completed the final step, which I took to mean the review of firing tables to determine the distances reflected by the use of various charges?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: But in your statement you focus on two charges, that is -- and I'll just get some clarity on this if we can. You say that using the firing table data you estimated there were two likely charges because you assessed that -- or you would have expected the mortar round to be fired at an optimum charge which would lead to maximum damage in the target area. Not one where the impact velocity was high driving the explosion into the ground rather on the surface?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: So you were saying, then, that you found that the charges 1 and 2 in contrast to 3, 4, 5, and 6 were the ones you were focusing on, and those first two charges you recall would have put the distance in the area you indicated in paragraph 24(B)?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right. I would -- I guess at this stage I would -- it may not be clear from my statement, but it's important I guess to remind the Court, I did not keep notes from that incident. I don't have any reports or anything to refer to. So referring to my memory, I don't specifically recall which charges I concluded. I remember taking the data, entering the firing tables at the angle of impact, as would normally be done to complete that step of a crater analysis. And normally what you would do in that case is apply your gunnery knowledge to the situation, which I did, which is as I say a step for normal field crater analysis; and the results I came up with using that data would have been a possible area on the map that overlapped or straddled the confrontation line, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, there's -- even assuming for the moment that persons who -- responsible for firing the projectile made the assessment that you did, that is, wanted to use the lowest charge for the purpose of the -- for purpose of maximum damage and have the lowest impact velocity, that would in any event depend on the location of the mortar unit or battery. In other words, some -- depending on where a mortar battery is, it's going to have to use a certain charge to reach the target area depending on its distance from that target area; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's part of the analysis in the selection of the optimum charge, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear. I would think that the primary and fundamental aspect of selection of the optimum charge is that it's going to reach the target?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: At a minimum, yes --

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. And if the battery is located at a certain distance from that target, it's going to dictate that you need a certain kind of charge, that you won't use charge 1 or 2, you'll have to use 3, 4, 5, or 6 . That's obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact if you find yourself at a distance where you have to use a charge that's going to increase the impact velocity, there are pretty time-tested ways of affecting the -- when that explosion occurs short of moving your mortar thousands of metres closer to the target; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes. In calculating the gunnery solution at the firing point, there are a number of factors that would be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well -- and among the factors, the availability and existence of various kinds of fuses or various adjustments to fuses; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be from a delayed fuse, a delayed impact, to a super-quick impact, to a proximity impact, which would actually have the projectile exploding even before it made contact; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the effect of impact velocity, there are some indications or pretty time-tested indication of impact velocity in this case, isn't there? And wouldn't that be, in fact, the fact the stabiliser went into the ground so deeply? Doesn't that, that is, the fact that the mortar tail fin, the stabiliser, was embedded deep in the crater impact -- or indicate a high-impact velocity?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: If you accept that that's the case, then absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, do you accept that that's the case?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: It's one of the possibilities, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And that would indicate a higher charge, correct, to create that greater impact velocity?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, the terminal ballistics in that case would be a very high velocity.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on, Mr. Joudry, to the conclusion or opinion or assessment you make with respect to the possibility of roof-top delivery, as it's stated at the bottom of page 5 of your statement. And you say there that -- basically at paragraph 24(C). If the aim was to have the mortar explode at the market, then the most accurate way to have achieved that was to launch the projectile by hand from a nearby roof-top. And first of all, let me -- and you go on to say that -- at paragraph 26, that among the factors you considered in reaching the view that the projectile might have been or was likely to have been -- by the way, what's your view on that? Do you think it was probably? Maybe? Are you throwing that out as a possibility, or do you have an assessment of its likelihood, that is, that it was hand-launched from a nearby building?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, to be clear, it may not be -- in hindsight it may not be entirely clear from my statement, sir, but what I have done and represented here in 24(B) at the time I completed that statement that -- sorry, the final step of the analysis to demonstrate to the UNPROFOR officials that in a normal field crater analysis you have to follow the data that you've accepted, which they hadn't done and I did from a gunnery perspective. However, I did advise them that given my assessment without even seeing the crater, the information I had in a normal field situation the analysis probably would have been discarded because it wouldn't have provided sufficient information to reach a conclusion in a normal field setting. So it wasn't that I had concluded that it was likely -- either (B) was likely or (C) was more likely, these were simply alternative solutions to the conclusion for the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at that alternative solution to the crater analysis that you offer, the roof-top delivery. First of all, just to -- you are aware that the officials who were actually on the scene came to the specific conclusion that that was not a possibility, that they said: "It is certain that it," that is the mortar bomb, "was not hand-launched from a building nearby." And that's found at P1441 at e-court page 25. You're aware that the people who were actually at the scene in examining all the evidence came to a conclusion that specifically excluded your option?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I recall reading that in one of the analysis by one individual, that's correct. But in my opinion at the time there was no clear evidence that would exclude that option in my mind.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, you say that one of the factors that led you to consider that option was the fact that there were high buildings in the immediate area of the explosion, and that's found at paragraph 25. Perhaps I can call up P14 -- P1709, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could enlarge the photograph on the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Joudry, the arrow is pointing to the area of the explosion or the crater, so could you just point out the -- whether these -- this photograph depicts any of the high buildings that you were referring to in paragraph 26?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at the time I had -- I didn't have access to a photograph of this nature. The one I had was a diagram and it looks like those buildings there were represented, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be, for example, the building to the immediate right of the picture and then the ones immediately behind?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. And those appear to be buildings of five or more storeys; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- from the pictures and the measurements, it looked like they were like five storeys or so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'll get back to that in a moment, but let me look at some of the other factors upon which you relied in focusing on this alternative explanation. First of all, you stated that one of the factors you considered was that there had been no reports of -- that the area had been subjected to intense targeting, bracketing of indirect fire, hours or even days prior to the explosion; and thus, for a single mortar to hit the market-place would have been virtually impossible. That's at paragraph 24(C) of your statement.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes. My -- just to amplify that, if -- if it was assumed that this was an aimed round, projectile, to hit the market that day, then to do so with one mortar round fired in isolation would be virtually impossible to have achieved that. That's what I meant by that.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: So that's based on the assumption that the mortar was -- that was aimed at that exact spot where it landed?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the -- that would be the assumption to enter that conclusion; right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And that assumption would not be valid, therefore, if the mortar was aimed at the general vicinity of the market, for example?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Secondly, I take it you were not aware of the fact or -- that the market had indeed been targeted before and that mortar rounds had landed very close to the market, that is, within a few metres?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I was aware of that from the UNPROFOR operations reports, that's right, but not in the immediate time-frame of the explosion on the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. So ten to twelve times during the last three months?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That sounds about right, yeah. And in gunnery terms, that would be called harassing fire.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, you also stated that among the factors you considered was the disturbance of the asphalt area -- asphalt surface in several areas. That's at paragraph 26 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Do you -- I appreciate the fact that you don't have notes and may not have reviewed the UNPROFOR materials, but do you have any recollection of who allegedly identified a disturbance of the asphalt surface in several areas?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant I guess by that statement. There were a number of -- in my opinion, there were a number of inconsistencies with the information that I was reviewing with regards to the crater analyses, and one of them was the -- one of the photographs that I had clearly indicated that the asphalt in the market area was broken and disturbed probably from just normal use over many years. And there was no indication of what the area of the crater looked like prior to the explosion. That was the point I was making there.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Mr. Joudry, are you aware that there was repeated assessment by those who were physically present at the scene and examined the scene that the shape of the crater and the shrapnel pattern were very clearly defined and very definitively indicative of a mortar bomb?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: That's not my recollection of the information I reviewed, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, let me look at a few of the -- assess few of the references here. First of all, at P1441, e-court page 23, looking toward the bottom. "From the shape of the crater, it is clearly evident that it has been formed by the explosion of a mortar bomb." If we turn to e-court page 18: "The shape of the crater is also consistent with the normal impact of a mortar bomb." E-court page 24: "Definite shape of the crater, spray of the fragments, and place of hitting of splinters to the dead and wounded clearly reveals that the type of burst was ground burst." Next page in e-court: "The crater was a classic mortar crater with a front edge undercut and the back edge grooved by splinters." And page 28 in e-court: "The lateral spray which was clean and sharp, had been produced by direct impact on the ground ..." And then further down: "The crater is clean and very sharply defined." These are all references, Mr. Joudry, to the assessment of those who were actually at the scene about the clarity of the crater in the context of a mortar bomb and of the shrapnel pattern.

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I don't recall reading that information at the time I did my review, sir. All I can say is that if that -- that was not the information that I had at my disposal for the review by UNPROFOR officials, most of whom had seen the crater, been on the scene within minutes, hours, or days after the explosion. Many of them, from my recollection from reading their reports, had considerable difficulty assessing the crater. In fact, I recall -- I don't have any of that information in front of me, sir, but one of the reports I recall -- one of the initial reports indicated it was clearly a low-angle trajectory and that one other report indicated that it may have even -- the projectile may have exploded at a -- on a table a metre off the ground. And clearly from looking at the photographs that I had, there was -- the crater itself was not as defined as those statements you just read me, but as I said I just looked at the information I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, let me suggest that that may -- that those factors that you just cited appear to reflect a review of the available evidence that focused somewhat selectively. So first with respect to the low-angle trajectory, I take it that that's a reference to Captain Verdy's report, where he mentioned something to the effect of low angle. Were you also aware that Captain Verdy in the same page of the document in the UNPROFOR report - it's all contained at P1441 - in which he mentioned low angle also reported an angle of descent of 1400 mils, that is, 78 degrees?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I -- that sounds about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Right, that's not a low angle, is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, it's not, but what he was talking about was the -- that was part of the inconsistencies I was referring to. You can't have a low-angle trajectory and create a crater that looks like that if you've got the high angle. So that was part of the discrepancy that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Mr. Joudry, did you not read that all of the UNPROFOR -- official UNPROFOR team recognised that Captain Verdy made mathematical or arithmetical miscalculations and also referred to a howitzer firing table rather than a mortar firing table and that that explained those discrepancies. Did you not read that?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I read that he made mathematical errors. I didn't read where anybody had made an attempt to correct his math to come up with a -- to follow the logic in what he was trying to say. But once again, I'm not disputing any of the information that was gathered that day. I simply tried to put it in perspective of a normal crater analysis so that the individuals receiving the information would not draw incorrect or inaccurate conclusions, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: You also alleged or you also asserted with -- in -- as one of the supporting features in your alternative explanations of what might have happened a reference at paragraph 26 to the "alleged tail fin having changed hands."

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that your use of the word "alleged" in that case is supposed to throw doubt on the -- whether or not the tail fin that was examined is, in fact, a tail fin associated with this particular mortar projectile?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Sir, I've already testified that I didn't see any of the parts of the projectile, any of the evidence that you're referring to. I simply read material and saw photographs, so I can't say that I -- that the tail -- with certainty that the -- any tail fin was actually recovered. I'm just saying that the information I had suggested there was a tail fin recovered from the crater.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And the information that was available to you through the UNPROFOR reports indicated quite clearly that the tail fin had a serial number on it which was recorded before it was provided to the Bosnian authorities and that it was later examined when it was recovered from the Bosnian authorities by UNPROFOR officials, including the FreBat team, which confirmed that it was the same tail fin; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: I'll defer to the wisdom of the Court in that area. As I said, all I can say is from the information I had there was a tail fin. I didn't see it or didn't touch it. There were -- part of the discrepancy in my mind that I relayed to UNPROFOR officials, I just wanted to caution them on making sure that we were all talking about the same tail fin, that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to the -- then the execution of this alternative or the alleged -- potential execution of this alternative theory. Now, you've indicated that the -- this is about the mortar having been thrown from one of the adjacent high buildings. Can you -- how is that done exactly? I mean, is it -- does the person who hand-launches the projectile control the line of direction in any way? How does the person throw it and how does the projectile land?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to sit slightly back from the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as you can appreciate, I've never actually performed that operation. What I was doing with this particular scenario was -- and the reason I had arrived at it as a possibility in the first case was that there were many -- in my mind there were many inconsistencies in the field crater analysis to that point. And one of the -- one of the possibilities I opined was that, well, what if, and the what if scenario was that it could have been launched in some way from a nearby roof-top. There was no indication in any of the reports I had reviewed that anybody made any effort to look at the roof-tops. There was no indication that anybody reported on the temperature of the -- around the crater or the temperature of the tail fin immediately after it had been recovered. In a normal situation like that if it was touched within minutes of the explosion, it would still be very hot. So one of the alternative solutions I offered was that it could have been launched in some way from a nearby roof-top, that could have been a fuse attached to the mortar bomb and it simply lobbed over the building by one or more individuals or with or without the assistance of some type of mechanism and that's how it would have been arrived at its point of detonation.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Right. And so my question to you was: Does the person lobbing this projectile control its line of direction?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Inasmuch as a human being could control the hand launch of anything, whether it be a baseball or whatever, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: What about the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, I would presume that if they were lobbing the projectile of that, it probably would have been lobbed outwards and upwards and the tail fin -- the stabiliser on it would have then stabilised the projectile as it descended to its point of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Colonel -- sorry to interrupt, Mr. Tieger. But before I forget to ask the question, can you assist us as to the approximate weight of 120-millimetre shell, that mortar round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically, Your Honour, but it would be in the actual -- the actual weight of the explosion would be in the order -- the weight of the explosive material would be about a hundred pounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So you've got to add the weight of the explosive to the weight of the casing and presumably that will vary according to the type of -- the manufacturer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would estimate that -- that it would probably be in the order of 120 pounds all up, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Did you estimate the distance between the buildings and the -- well, let me go to P1440, pages 5 and 6. And actually, I'm going to return there in a second, but before I do let me go quickly to P5921 page 5, line 5. In -- just to -- this is an indication on some firing tables of the shell mass with and without the fuses, ranging between 12 kilos -- well, for particularly light between 10 kilos without the fuse to 15 or 16 kilos. And I would also note for the Court that at P1973 we see an estimate of the mass of the shell at 12.6 kilos. So with either of those figures in mind, Mr. Joudry, whether it's 12 and a half kilos to a hundred pounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn back to P1440, again at pages 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, in the diagram to the right, number 5, we see that tall building that you identified in the photograph earlier, that was that tall five- or six-storey building that was adjacent to the general area of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we can -- that's number 5. And if we could turn to the legend at page 2 we can clarify that. That's the 22nd December building, the height of which is about 15 and a half metres. That would be page 2 where you can see the key. Well, let's move forward then.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Mr. Joudry, would you accept that the diagram of that area indicates that the shortest distance, that is, the directly adjacent distance between that building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Were you referring to pages 6 -- key is appearing on page 6 in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not page 2. Footnote 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're correct. What I was looking for at page 2 - and not very artfully - was the indication that the distance between the December 22nd building and the impact site was 11.1 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And I can show that to you, Mr. Joudry, but I presume you're -- you will accept that?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's reasonable. I haven't -- as I said, I didn't take any -- I don't have any notes to refer to and it's difficult to reconstruct my knowledge from 18 years ago, but that sounds about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I guess the question I want to ask you then is a follow-up to His Honour Judge Morrison's question, and in order to ask that I may need to approach the witness with an item, Mr. President. We saw -- you estimated that the weight of the object -- the projectile was about a hundred pounds. We looked at indications in the materials that it was at least 12 and a half pounds. I have here an item I'd like to show you. This is a 12-kilogramme object and I'd like you to just -- I'd like to approach you with this and ask you a question if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I'm fascinated to see what you could ask the witness to actually do with it, Mr. Tieger, but in principle in the absence of any objection from the Defence, I don't think we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: We can assume that [indiscernible] of the Defence, there is no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: My microphone doesn't seem to be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Our microphones didn't seem to be working. In any event, there is no objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Joudry, you're welcome to hoist that in any way you want or move it around. It has a handle so it's considerably easier to manipulate than most items of 12 kilogrammes, and it's at least lighter than the weight of the projectile. But with that actually physically in front of you, can you tell the Judges if you really consider that it's possible to hand -- to throw this thing 11 metres?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, in short, yes of course. You have to remember that if -- in order for the projectile to be hand-launched from the top of the building it wouldn't have to go out 11 metres, it would have to arrive at the point on the ground which is 11 metres from the building. So that was possible in my mind. I would have done the calculations. I can't reconstruct them for you here today, but it's a simple mathematical calculation on the triangle. So that would have been possible, and in my mind and in my opinion - as it was then, as it remains today - it would have been possible for one or several individuals with or without the assistance of some type of mechanism to launch a 120-millimetre mortar from the top of a building.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Do you know what the weight of an Olympic shot put is?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, I know the weight -- no, I don't, but I know the weight of a 155-millimetre projectile, many of which I have lifted in the past, and I'm quite familiar with the weight of projectiles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can bring this up to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It won't be necessary, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And then having hurled or lobbed, as you said, this over-12-kilogramme object 11 metres, so it would have -- would it have landed at an angle of descent that the lobber could calculate or would it be entirely random in your view?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: It would have been relatively random, noting that it would have been lobbed from the top of the building which was approximately, as you have pointed out, 15 or 16 metres off the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: So it could have landed then at an angle that would have entirely excluded the possibility of any mortar shell, either 90 degrees because of the aerodynamics of a mortar or 2 or 3 degrees; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about the 2 or 3 degrees, but it could have landed at an awkward angle. And one of the things I would remind you of is getting back to the number of discrepancies that I saw at the time reading the reports, it was clear that many of the initial UNPROFOR officials on the ground had difficulty reading the shrapnel pattern and -- which led me to think of: Well, what are the other alternatives? That's why I started to think of this one as a possible option.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And then since you assert that the lobber would then have had to physically insert the stabiliser into the ground after the explosion, that person would have to figure out what the approximate angle of descent had randomly been to put the stabiliser back in at an angle that was consistent with the shrapnel splinter pattern; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: No, not at all, and that's one of the things I pointed to in my discrepancies or the -- noted in many of the discrepancies around the crater. All the -- in this particular alternative solution, some person would have to insert the tail fin at an angle to make sure that it looked like it was at least above the top of the building.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: So that would have to be some predetermined angle or an angle decided upon right at that very moment of inserting this item into the ground?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: It wouldn't have been predetermined. I would have imagined in this case they would have -- the person or persons responsible if this alternative was in actual case what happened, is that clearly they would have known roughly where the projectile would have landed within close proximity to the building, and all they would have had to do was make sure that the angle looked like it appeared that the tail fin cleared the top of the nearest building.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
