utterances.text: But that assumes that the shrapnel pattern which was randomly created would be consistent with that and that was entirely impossible to predict according to you, so that the whole project is fraught with the inherent inconsistency between or potential inconsistency between the shrapnel pattern, which can't be controlled according to you, and the insertion of the stabiliser in a manner that indicates it could have cleared the building?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: In my opinion - and as I said, I did not see the crater - the pictures that I saw as well as the statements by the UNPROFOR officials who were there on the ground initially, clearly they had difficulty assessing the crater. And if these were analysts trained to some degree in crater analysis, then if they had difficulty with the initial assessment of the splinter pattern, then that in my mind presented an inconsistency and therefore the projectile could have virtually landed on the ground at almost any angle.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: And then, according to your theory, in between the very few minutes that it took for the first UNPROFOR official to arrive - five minutes as we saw estimated in the UNPROFOR report before - if not the arrival of other officials before then, that someone would have had to insert the stabiliser into the ground. How is that done under your theory?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: It would have been done in the same way as it would have been done under the original theory, which is somebody inserting the tail fin into the ground, if it could be re-inserted and measured, then it certainly could be inserted on the first occasion in my mind.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: Well, the re-insertion was into a hole created by a high-impact velocity, but let's take a look at the ground and the depth of that stabiliser. And perhaps we can look at P1711 and we need to go to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE UNPROFOR AND OTHER
utterances.text: We've just seen a clip that went from about 8.55 to about 9.21 showing the stabiliser being cleared away by FreBat IV, and we see here the depth of the crater and the extent to which it's lodged into the soil. So according to your theory, Mr. Joudry, someone ran out after the explosion in the midst of the dead and dying victims and plugged this stabiliser into the ground unseen before UNPROFOR arrived or any Bosnian police officials arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No further questions to this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly, Your Excellencies. Could we please see P01441, which we have already seen. Could we have it up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for it to appear, Colonel, my -- Mr. Tieger reminded you of the fact that there were shells, some shells, earlier. But you said there weren't any on that day. Why is it important for there to have been shells on that day? When and under what conditions are firing elements, in fact, or firing criteria established, determined?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: In this case, one of the theories is that it was an aimed round and the explosion was meant to go off in the market that day. Following that logic, in order for that to have happened with indirect fire it would have had to have been targeted and bracketed very precisely, keeping in mind that indirect fire is not a precise weapon, it's an area weapon. And for one particular round to have been aimed, particularly a mortar, aimed and fired and to have hit the market that day would be in my opinion highly unlikely. And one of the things that I looked at was I went back through the UNPROFOR operations reports to determine if there had been that type of bracketing in that area immediately prior to explosion, and I recall going back several days and noting that while there had been come explosions they weren't in the market itself, which led me to the conclusion that it was not a bracketed and recorded target by the firing unit that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 715. We have 705 here, but could we see 715 in this document. The ERN number 715.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 32, Mr. Tieger stressed that two UNPROFOR officials in fact visited the site. Could I now ask you to have a look at item 17 in this document. You can read it to yourself. And could you tell us whether these UN officials arrived at a conclusion that is consistent with the conclusion that you arrived at? [In English] Particularly the last question -- the last sentence: "There is insufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb in question could have been fired by either side."

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Overall, my conclusion was exactly the same as that. I simply went on to caution the UNPROFOR officials that not only was it impossible to prove, in fact they were using crater analysis in an inappropriate manner in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 724 in this same document, that would be some nine pages before this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Conclusions." Bullet point 5. We are talking about a different UNPROFOR team now. Please take a look at (d). I'm going to read so that everybody can hear it. [In English] "It is not possible to determine the exact range from the firing point to the target with mortars. The range lies in the region of 300 metres to 5.551 metres, which is the published data for the M49P1." [Interpretation] Did this team arrive at conclusions similar to yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one potential misstatement. I don't know what the accused means by a different team, but he's citing the same report just a different portion. So if he's trying to suggest that we're dealing with -- if he means different from this witness, I leave it alone. If he means we're now going to an entirely different report rather than a restatement of the same thing he just looked at, then I do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, we saw that the document was signed by one team and there were nine different investigations, which you can also see in this document. The first signatories were Gauthier, Karen [phoen] and Jansen [phoen] and I can't read the rest, and further on we can see that an analysis follows in the same document; however, the conclusion was arrived at by a different team. So this document was not created by one single team. This is a compilation of all the elements that United Nations dispatched on the 15th of February as their joint conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All I would like to hear from you, Witness, is whether conclusion (d) is consistent with what you concluded yourself?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Not exactly, sir. I remember reading this report, and as I pointed out in my statement, the UNPROFOR officials who had done the crater analysis and the ones who had compiled this report did not complete the last step. So if you have an angle of fall, which they clearly did to some degree of accuracy, or an angle of impact, then the next step is what does that angle of impact relate to in terms of a possible charge and therefore a range, and then you apply that to a map and ask yourself: Does this make sense with the other information that I have. So the UNPROFOR officials did not complete that final step. So the range -- so I did simply with the flawed -- what I considered to be flawed information to demonstrate to the UNPROFOR officials that there is another step in this crater analysis technique that they were using, inappropriately nonetheless. And I don't recall the specific range that I came up with, but I do recall that when I plotted those shorter ranges on a map it came up with an area that straddled the confrontation line and about 5 per cent of that possible area was on the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation line. So I took that range and narrowed it using the final step of crater analysis to come up with one of those possibilities that I indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 731 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read just the first sentence. [In English] "The estimation of the range based upon the study of a crater analysis of a mortar round cannot be accurate in any case. The only information that can be obtained from the crater is the angle of descent, and from this datum with the firing tables of the mortar we will be ..." it's not legible but ... [Interpretation] Do you agree with this part of the conclusion as well?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Absolutely, and this refers to my concern with how the -- the limitations of crater analysis and what it was originally designed for in terms of gunnery, and that is basically to -- not to assign culpability but to narrow down possible locations from which enemy weapons may be firing such that you could follow-up and determine location by a more accurate means. There are -- of the critical elements in a crater analysis, if you have the angle of descent you can then use that for the final step. If you don't have an angle of descent, then obviously you can't complete the final step. But even in that case all it gives you is a possible range of locations in an area in which the weapon might have been fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now 727, page 1, just one more sentence. (B)4, or rather, bullet point 4(b): [In English] "The crater analysis has been conducted seven days after the occurrence of the incident. This crater formed by the bomb has been tempered time and again by various personnel." [Interpretation] Is this in keeping with your conclusions about the accuracy which is questionable?

utterances.speaker: STEVEN JOUDRY
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the several major concerns that I had expressed to the UNPROFOR officials with regards to the disturbance of the crater which was at the very least led -- should lead some high degree of question in the results that they were looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Joudry, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for your coming to The Hague. You are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I wish the Court well in your deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joudry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D04879 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Russell. Thank you for coming here to testify. May I ask you to tell us whether you have reviewed the statement which is now on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I've reviewed that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this statement accurate? Does it reflect your words accurately?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, it reflects my words accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom, would your answers be identical to the ones provided in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender the statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter as well as three attached or associated documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to the last document, which is 1D4517, while the document itself was admitted as -- already, but the reason for the Defence in tendering this document is because of the witness's handwritten notes. Am I correct in so understanding, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they will all be admitted. Shall we give the number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement 65 ter 1D04879 will be Exhibit D2364. 65 ter number 1D4515 will be Exhibit D2365. 65 ter number 1D4516 will be Exhibit D2366. And 65 ter number 1D4517 will be Exhibit D2367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read the short summary of Mr. Russell's statement in English. [In English] Mr. John Russell is a retired officer of the armed forces of Canada. In February 1994 he was working for UNPROFOR in Sarajevo as military assistant to Sergio de Mello. While in Sarajevo, Major Russell was called upon to do crater analysis on several occasions. On 5th of February, 1994, he was tasked to go to the scene of the explosion at the Markale. He arrived at the scene between 16 -- 15 past 16 and 30 past 16. He located the crater and got down on the knee to conduct a quick crater analysis. He noted that the dead and injured had been removed from the scene and that this process disturbed much of the evidence, such as location of fragments. The entire area appeared to have been swept thoroughly. Major Russell was able to determine the approximate direction of the fire by examining the splash pattern of the round on the asphalt and using a compass. He concluded that the round had come from the east/north-east. The UN investigative team report notes that the -- he arrived at the measurement of 450 mils. The UN investigative team report also notes that he measured the angle of descent at 1.200 to 1.300 mils. While on his knee at the crater, Major Russell was struck by how steep on the angle and that the round must have come in on the clear and large building adjacent to the crater. This led him to believe that the round had come from a location closer to the crater than a round fired from further away. However, based upon the fact that the round could have been fired with zero to six charges, he concluded that it was not possible to determine the distance that the round had travelled. Since both parties occupied positions in the direction from which the round had come, he could not be certain which side had fired the round. Major Russell examined the hole made by the projectile but did not measure its depth. He noticed that debris had fallen into the hole and did not believe that the depth of the hole at the time of impact could be accurately determined by the time he arrived on the scene or that the depth of the hole could help determine where the round had come from. He does not believe that re-inserting the tail fin into the hole would provide an accurate measurement of the angle of descent since the hole had been disturbed in the intervening period. Major Russell also indicated that the fact that a tail fin is found in the ground does not necessarily establish that the round had travelled a long distance than if the tail fin had been found somewhere in the area. There are too many variables to draw that conclusion. In all his experience with crater analysis, the speed of which -- at which the round hits the ground had never been an issue. Major Russell recalled hearing it reported on the CNN on the evening of 5th of February, 1994, that the Bosnian Serbs had shelled the market. He believed that this was the result of propaganda and that from then on it would be widely believed that the Bosnian Serbs had fired the shell regardless of the true facts. Major Russell kept a personal diary during his time in the former Yugoslavia. In an entry dated 5th of February, 1994, he wrote: "At around 12.10, a shell hit in the market-place in the old town, and as I write, (0015, 6 February) the count is 68 dead and 198 wounded. It is the biggest single kill of people ever in 22 months. I was at the site to do a quick crater analysis, and although I agree with the direction that the round came from, I disagree with the distance, believing that the BH shot at themselves. Many here don't want to think of this as there are a lot of casualties, but I think otherwise." Some days after the explosion, Major Russell accompanied some UN personnel to the basement of a building in Sarajevo where the Bosniak side kept mortars. One of the UN personnel had the tail fin recovered from the Markale explosion with him. When they arrived, they asked the person in charge if they had any 120-millimetre mortars. He said no. Then one of the UN group opened a box and found 120-millimetre mortars. The mortars in the box were hand manufactured. Major Russell compared the manner of welding of the 120-millimetre mortars to the manner of welding of the tail fin from the market and they looked to be the same calibre, colour, and to have been welded in the same way. At that stage I don't have additional questions for Major Russell, so Madam West is free to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, coming back to the last document, i.e., the 1D4517, you confirmed that you're tendering that document because of the handwritten notes by Mr. Russell. But all he said in his statement was that he made some notations without telling what it is about. I'm not sure that we can read his comment without his assistance. So in order for you to tender that document you need to put some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. If we can call up 1D4517, Dr. Karadzic can put some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the bottom part with the handwritten portion be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major Russell, is this your handwritten note?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwritten note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read that note aloud for the benefit of everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The note says: "This may no longer be true," this is related to the statement above it, "but if it came from the team's inspection. If fin was stuck in ground, then no above ground explosion occurred."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, are things clearer now? Can we please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you put --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- have the next page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- two question marks at the end of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is for you, Major. The Judge has asked you whether you put the two question marks on this page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did put those two question marks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And meaning what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meaning, Your Honour, that it was something that I had wondered about and basically the statement above is related to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, could you please read this note of yours aloud.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: This note says: "This would happen anyway."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, have I laid enough foundation for the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would this mean, that this would happen anyway? What's the point of that comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that relates to the point about the maximum shrapnel disposition or dispersion and projectiles of all kinds causing serious damage and death in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we take a break now? We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.28 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Russell.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for meeting me yesterday. I think this will provide some clarity today, but one thing I would like to say before we start: Since we both speak the same language we need to be careful that we speak slowly. On the screen in front of you, you're going to see a transcript, and it goes simultaneously, and it may be helpful for you to keep an eye on that transcript to sort of guide you on how slowly we speak. So, sir, you were in Sarajevo from December 1993 to April 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's a total of about four months; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That's about -- yeah, four and a -- four months, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at paragraph 7 of your statement you said that your first experience with crater analysis was when you were with the UN. Was that first experience the crater at the market-place on February 5th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you also speak in your statement about other occasions in which you did analysis, that's paragraph 9. And I counted that up and that appears to be about six other occasions. Can you please tell us of those occasions how many of them were before your analysis at the market-place in early February?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, at least five.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So subsequent to February and the time you left, it's your testimony then that you only did one other analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: After the Sarajevo one, the market one, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And if we now focus on February 5th. When you arrived at the market-place, were you aware that other analysis had already been done?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any other crater analysis before the one I was conducting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you now know that there had been an analysis at 12.30 by the locals. There had been one at approximately 12.45 by FreBat. And then Captain Verdy had also done an examination about 3.00. And it was about 4.30 when you came in; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I knew about -- I didn't know about the locals, but I did know about the other two. And yes, approximately 4.30 is about the time I got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And you will agree with me that there was only one explosion at the market-place that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So any fragmentation from -- shrapnel fragmentation that would have been found on that day would have been the remnants of only one shell; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And yesterday when we spoke you told me that shrapnel fragmentation could be used to determine the calibre of a shell. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now paragraph 15 and 17 of your report, if we can turn the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we ask the Registry to provide a hard copy to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you have your report D2364 in front of you; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And focusing your attention on paragraph 15, in this paragraph you are giving a quote of the report you had written at the time, and in it you say: "It's most important that the site should not be disturbed." And then you go on about the things that would be found on a site. And then your last sentence is: "This obviously disturbed much of the evidence, such as location of fragments." So when you came on the scene, you could not find any shrapnel fragments; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I initially looked for big fragments and I couldn't find any obviously, and I went into the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And if we go to paragraph 17 this is something that you continue to talk about, and you say that when you were interviewed by the UN team: "I concluded that the entire area had been swept thoroughly. I looked around for shrapnel and did not find anything." Major Russell, why was the importance -- or what was the importance of examining the shrapnel at the scene when you knew there was only one shell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: It's important to determine the calibre of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, putting aside that we knew -- putting aside that particular fact, is there any other reason that it would have been important?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So you say it's important for determining the calibre of the shell. Is there any other reason why collecting the fragmentation would be important to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, it would confirm the calibre, and from that you can look at range tables to determine the distance, minimum/maximum range.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you know on this occasion part of the projectile itself was found in the hole; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Now I do, but at the time I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the fact that there was no shrapnel there for you to analyse in this particular occasion, since we know what the calibre was, has no bearing at all on your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Ask me that question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me ask it another way. It wasn't so well stated. I'm interested in why in your report from recent times, after you know everything that happened at the time, in paragraph 17 you focus on the lack of shrapnel and you've confirmed to us that shrapnel is important to discover -- figure out the calibre of the shell. But in the case today as you know it, we don't have to figure out the calibre of the shell because we know what it is. So will you agree with me that in these specific circumstances the fact that the fragmentation had already been swept away by the time you got there made no difference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I don't agree, and the reason for that is the imprint on the ground can also indicate the size of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. And that's exactly what we're about to move to. One of the important things regarding shrapnel, would you agree with me, is not the shrapnel itself but it's the imprint the shrapnel makes on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so when you arrived on the scene, you looked at a pattern that you saw on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at paragraph 18 - we see this on the screen in your report - you say when you examined the crater: "I observed that the imprint left by the crater was smaller than I would have expected, leading me to believe that the round may have struck an object such as a table before hitting the ground." Yesterday when we spoke we talked about this, and the Trial Chamber knows now from looking at your report that you've edited that you later discovered in fact that the tail fin was embedded in the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so as a result of finding out that information, you changed your opinion; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I changed my opinion of where the round started to explode. In other words, I changed my opinion that the round was initiated prior to going into the ground by an object above the ground. I changed that on that note, as I was now convinced based on that information that indeed the round did strike the ground and it exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have D2367, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What you're going to see before you in a moment is the report you spoke about earlier with the accused. Do you see that on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I believe they should bring up the comments. I don't see the whole comments there I think that you're referring to. Or, I see the -- I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is a report that you wrote later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I wrote this report the day after. To my recollection, it was the day after I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so that would be February 6th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the handwritten notes that we saw earlier today, those handwritten notes, how much later did you write those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we scroll down the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I do not know. I don't know. I wrote them but I don't know exactly when I wrote them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that you wrote them at least subsequent to reading the report of the team of UN experts that came in several days later?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If we can focus on the first paragraph and we see it already, in the middle of that paragraph it says: "Normally a good crater analysis can be done due to the fact that when a mortar round impacts on the ground, a specific signature assists the investigations [sic] in determining the approximate direction from which it came, and the angle of descent." Now, I can see here you're saying that the crater is helpful in determining bearing; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But it also appears that you're saying the crater is helpful in determining angle of descent, and my question for you is: Do you mean the splash pattern is helpful in determining the angle of descent or do you mean any hole that's created?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, both play together, the pattern giving you direction and then inside the crater where the hole is, being able there to put in a measuring device or adjusting it with a measuring device to give you an angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So let's first speak about the bearing. Since this is the only report we have from you, and looking over this it does not specifically talk about methodology, can you just tell the Court now: How is it that you determined bearing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, you place a number of stakes at both ends of the splash about the left and the right, and then you also put two stakes in the middle of that imprint. And then you shoot the bearing back in the middle so you've got -- you know, you make a 90-degree angle in that particular splash and then you measure the bearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So you no longer have your actual measurements; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I don't have any document that shows my calculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's fine and we can go to a document later that records that. But did you use a compass at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you use magnetic north for your measurements?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, there was a magnetic declination already input into my compass for that area in the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can just go to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you'll see it in a moment, but on the second page, the last paragraph, it says: "Based on the evidence available at the site, the minimum and maximum range at which the weapon system could have been fired straddles the confrontation line. It is therefore impossible to determine with certainty on which side of the confrontation line the round was fired." So, Major Russell, at this point again we have no indication of the methodology you used. Can you please tell the Court now how is it that you determined angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: You -- once you measure the angle of descent, you refer back to range tables, and then those range tables for that particular calibre will give you a minimum and maximum range of that round based on whatever charge was used for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And we can back up a little bit here. My question for you is: On this specific occasion tell us exactly the steps you took to measure angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Based on our discussions yesterday, basically I don't remember doing it. I don't remember measuring the angle of descent, I don't remember that, but I've done them before. And based on the calculations that were provided in the board of inquiry, this was the first time I said: Oh, look, I did do an angle of descent but I don't remember doing one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. You just said you had done them before. So let's talk about what your habit was in terms of angle of descent. How did you do them before?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: You normally -- you normally go to the deepest part in the crater, where the nose normally goes in, and you put in a stake there. And then, you know, you keep it on the bearing that you've discovered. You put the stake there and then you use a protractor and you measure the angle at which it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And yesterday when we had this discussion you said that normally you used a 12-inch nail as your stake; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I used to carry with me a number of 12-inch nails, a string, and a plumb-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: And something to drive them into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So then would it be fair to say that on this occasion to get angle of descent it was most likely that you took that nail, inserted it into the hole in the ground, and then used a protractor to get the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If we can go back to your report D2364, you have it in front of you, and go to page 4, please. Thank you. Now, at the top of this page this is where you have a discussion of the depth of the hole, and in paragraph 24 you said you examined the hole but that you didn't examine the depth. You noted that debris had fallen into it and you did not believe that the depth of the hole at the time of impact could be accurately determined by the time you had arrived or that the depth of the hole could help determine where the round had come from. And then in paragraph 25 you say: "I do not believe that re-inserting the tail fin into a hole would provide an accurate measurement of the angle of descent since the hole had been disturbed in the intervening period." Major Russell, can you tell us again about how you determined the angle of descent, what you did with the nail?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Okay. I put it into the nose cone -- there is a furrow there that -- where the tip of the round ends up at -- in the ground, and you try and find the deepest part in there and then you place the nail in. And that's how you would do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you took the nail and you put it in the hole and you measured the angle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 25 isn't that exactly what is happening here, re-inserting a tail fin into a hole to provide an angle of descent; isn't that exactly what you did?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The reason of this comment on 25 was that the embedment of the tail fin in the ground was the true measurement, but it was no longer there. And in some cases when you do crater analysis you do find imprints without tail fins. And that is the best procedure, lacking that embedded fin, to try and measure the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I'm speaking generally about the process, and the process as I understand it that you used was taking something, inserting it in the hole, and measuring the angle. And the process, as I understand it from paragraph 25 and what was done later, was that they took something, they stuck it in the hole, and they did certain calculations to measure the angle. Tell me what in the process is different between what you did and what they later did with the tail fin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I would think that the 12-inch nail is a smaller diameter and more pointed than the flat part of the tail fin that break -- you know, that would be there, I think, and then you have a better chance of finding the deepest part of that furrow. So that's -- to the best of my ability was to find that deepest part and find and -- and secure that nail in that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But everything you just said has nothing to do with suggesting that the procedure was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The procedure would be, as you said, inserting the tail fin would be the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: -- as me inserting the nail.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So then can we say that your paragraph 25 is perhaps not entirely accurate? Because here you say: "I do not believe that re-inserting the tail fin into the hole would provide an accurate ... angle of descent ..." And you just told us that you yourself re-inserted -- you inserted a nail and got an angle of descent. So would you agree with me that perhaps that's not entirely clear the way that it's articulated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I would agree it's not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. In 20 -- you go on to say that 26 -- in 26: "The fact that a tail fin is found in the ground does not necessarily establish that the round had travelled a longer distance than if the tail fin had been found" elsewhere ... "there are too many variables ..." And then in 27 you say: "In all my experience with crater analysis, the speed at which the round hits the ground has never been an issue." I want to talk to you for a moment here about speed, but firstly we know from a few minutes ago that you had seven crater analyses done in Sarajevo. And then later in your statement you also say you did a few in southern Lebanon in 2000 and 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so that would make about a total of nine analyses; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yeah. Maybe ten including the one when I was being trained on that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So the day and a half of training that you had in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So that's a total of nine. Tell us, when you were in Lebanon, the surface that you examined, was that a hard surface or a soft surface?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: It was both.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: One of each?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, there was about seven rounds in this particular event and some were in the ground, soft ground, and some were on a road.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So on -- of these ten occasions when we speak about all your experience, it's -- it encompasses those ten different times; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 1D05015, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now I'd like to talk about speed, and you say that in all your experience the speed at which the round hits the ground has never been an issue. We may go to page 3, please. Now, sir, you've not seen this before so I'm going to read this to you. This is a report from the Defence that regards this particular issue that we're talking about. And in paragraph 5.3 it talks about this issue of speed and it says: "In this instance the stabilising tail boom continued to travel forward because its rearward velocity caused by the explosion was less than the forward velocity of the mortar bomb. Thus the velocity at which the stabilising tail boom penetrated into the earth consisted of the impact velocity of the mortar bomb less the velocity at which the stabilising tail boom was ejected from the rear of the mortar bomb by the detonation of the explosive." I'm sure it's of no surprise to you to know that this paragraph was written in regard to this particular incident. And would you agree with me that it appeared in this paragraph, the person who wrote it certainly believes that the speed at which the round hits the ground is an issue, it's something that's important to determine?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The -- in our training, this was never considered. We always worked on the direction and the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So in your training in October of 1993 and in the ten times that you did an analysis, speed was something that you just didn't deal with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: It was never considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But you wouldn't discount that speed as something that might be important to an analysis, or perhaps you've just never done it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I've never done a crater analysis considering speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies, but if we can go back to his report which is D2364, looking at page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now I would like for us to talk about the angle of descent, and you do that on page 3, and it begins at paragraph 21, and it's the page before this. But specifically at paragraph 22 you speak about steepness and let's read that. It says: "While on my knee at the crater, I was struck by how steep of an angle that the round must have come in on to clear the large building adjacent to the crater. This led me to believe that the round had come from a location closer to the crater than a round fired ... further away." Now, we spoke about this a bit yesterday and you gave -- in explaining this to me you gave me an example of a water hose to illustrate your conclusion, that the steeper the angle, the closer the firing point. Can you tell the trial Court what you mean by that. Use the example of the water hose.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Okay. In the discussion I used the example of the water hose, saying placing a water hose at a 45-degree angle with the maximum flow on, you would see the water fly out and then gravity would pull it down to a certain location. If you pull -- if you push the fire hose down, the area where the water lands is closer. If you pull the hose up higher than 45 degrees, the water again starts to come closer. And when I looked at the steepness of the angle of descent, this is what I was reminded of.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have D2366, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the Court has heard evidence that at the time -- or heard in the summary that at the time of this incident you kept a diary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the evening of February 5th, I think this is in the early morning hours of February 6th, we see what you wrote. And on the left-hand side of this page - it's a little bit difficult to see but I'm going to read it, and you can tell me if I'm reading it correctly: "At around 12.10," so that day on the 5th, "a shell hit in the market-place in the old town and as I write," this is going to be 12.15 in the early morning hours of the 6th, "the count is 68 dead, 198 wounded. It is the biggest single hit of people ever in 22 months. I," not quite sure what it says here, "I was on its site to do a quick crater analysis, and although I agree with its direction that the round came from, I disagree with the distance believing that the BiH shot at themselves." Now, you wrote this that very night; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as we -- as we spoke yesterday you wrote this in your diary as a result of believing that the steep angle meant a closer firing point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to use Sanction at this point and we're going to be looking at a document that's already been admitted. It's P05921. And we'll be looking at e-court page 16, and this is a firing table. I believe it was admitted during the cross of a witness -- a previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you'll see this momentarily. And this is a firing table. I assume you're familiar with firing tables?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. This is a firing table for the projectile that was launched on the market-place. And we know that the shell was an M62P3, and we can highlight that and you'll see it on the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But first I just want to show you as we go across and everyone can see, we're seeing six charges. Are you familiar with this type of table?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I know this is the one that was used --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: -- for the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And so the green --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: But I was using a different range table.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. And that's fine. And we're just going to use this as an example.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: But it's -- works the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the green boxes that we see on the top now, those represent the charges, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. And now on the top you see shells to which it's applicable, and in this case it's applicable to M62P3. So what I'd like to show you regards the angle of descent that you came to. Now, at this point the Court has not seen that angle of descent on a report that you wrote. But yesterday we looked at it, and I think the angle of descent that you came to was 1.200 mils to approximately 1.300 mils.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So just for the purposes of an example, I'm in no way suggesting that that is the accurate angle of descent for this event, but for the purposes of this example what I did is went through each charge and found the angle of descent that was the closest to 1200. And so in the first case under charge 1 it's 1.218, and then I went across to get the distance, and that would be 900 metres. And then under the second charge we have 1.198, and at that charge for the shell we go over to get the distance and that would be 1.700. For the third charge, we have 1.203 and for the distance that would fire this shell at 2500 metres. For the fourth charge, 1.202 and that would fire 3.300 metres. The fifth charge -- excuse me, the fifth charge is 1.198 which would end up 4100 metres. And the sixth charge, 1.192 would end up at 4800 metres. Now, Major, after seeing this firing table where the angle of descent under each charge is the same and yet as the charges increase the distances increase, would you conclude that this -- the principle that this represents is not the principle you applied when you wrote in your diary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't -- ask me that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So after seeing this, can you agree with me that in each case I just showed you the angle of descent or the steepness was the same. In each charge it was approximately 1200 mils, yet the firing distance increased as the charges increase. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so this is not the principle you used when we looked at your diary and when we looked at your report. You concluded that because it was so steep you assumed it had to come from a close distance; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That's what I felt in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: -- that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's -- and it's because of that steepness and it's because of that principle, that's why you wrote it in your diary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that you applied an erroneous principle and you came to an incorrect conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: In that particular case of the diary, yes. In the particular case of the range tables, you can see the minimum and maximum range; and therefore, those minimum and maximum ranges cross the confrontation line and that's the official report that I put in on the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But that's not my question. If you had understood this principle to be exactly as it's related on the firing table, and not these exact figures, but the principle that it represents, would you have come to a different conclusion than you came to in your diary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You also in your statement spoke about the media and you said - this is D2364, page 5, it's paragraph 32 - you said: "That evening" -- in paragraph 32 you said you recalled hearing it reported on CNN that evening and you believed that this was a result of propaganda and that from then on it would be widely believed that the Serbs had fired the shell regardless of the true facts. When you heard that report, that was before you wrote in your diary; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Later on in the statement towards the bottom at 36 you talk about some days later in which you went -- you accompanied some UN personnel to the basement of a building. Now, "some days later," could this have been February 12th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, it was earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It was earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I believe it was about five days -- I think five days after.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I ask you that is in here it's footnoted a particular report referring to your visit and that visit is February 9th and that's four days later.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is it possible that that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so when you went on this visit, if we can go to the next page, 37, you stated: "When we arrived, we asked the person in charge if they had any 120-millimetre mortars," this must be shells, "and he said no. One of our group opened a box and we found 120-millimetre mortars. The mortars in the box were hand manufactured. I compared the manner of the welding of the 120-millimetre mortars to the manner of the welding on the tail fin from the market and they looked to be the same calibre, colour, and to have been welded in the same way." Major Russell. How long were you able to look at those mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Maybe five, ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were you able to pick them up and hold them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, I held one in my hand, a complete round.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is it your suggestion that these mortar shells that you found in that basement were from the same lot of the mortar shells used at -- on February 5th at the market-place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It is not your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about them in particular made you believe they were hand manufactured?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The one I held had no identification marks. It was roughly made on a lathe, and it had a free-floating firing pin at the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. How do you know it was roughly made on a lathe?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, when you pick it up you have all the rough edges on it and everything else, unlike a manufactured round.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I think you just said that there was no identification marks on it, so you couldn't see any writing on it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, no, I didn't see any writing on the round I held.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And are you aware that the stabiliser found at the market-place does have some writing on it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Are you also aware that the former Yugoslavia had a long history of weapons production?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You made that comparison. Did anyone else in the delegation make that same comparison?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No one did --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: We just looked at them and they looked similar and that was about as far as we went.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you're saying another person other than you thought they looked similar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yeah, the welding parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P1441. And may I have e-court page 49.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in your statement when you speak about this visit you reference this particular page that we're about to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: E-court page 49. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is the report that was generated from your visit, your visit and the other people at the visit as well. And under the assessment at the bottom it says: "The tail fins," here it says "finded" "found on the market-place and those that were shown to us later," referring to these two visits above, "were different from the others we saw today." Major Russell, the person who wrote this assessment does not come to the same conclusion that you did. This person comes to a different conclusion, which is that the mortars that you all saw that day were different than the one that was found at the market-place. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I -- when I first saw the tail fin, I believed it looked the same. But I have no problem in accepting the comment of this report which identifies batch lot numbers and stuff on the primer and the fuse. I didn't look at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Major. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, sir, do we agree that the fuses are not hand made? Can you actually tell us what can be hand made and what is made in a factory and supplied to the end users?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Not really. All I can say is if you have an original round you can copy it in a factory that has the machines to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the body of the shells that you saw in the cellar, were they forged or cast to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: They seemed to be forged, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, we heard some things from the Prosecutor today. Do any of them change your conclusion that it could not be established which of the two sides from which side of the confrontation line fired the shell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I have no doubt in my own mind that I was unable to determine the exact range and distance from which that round was fired because the minimum/maximum range straddled the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in this same document there are several conclusions arrived at by the United Nations which point to the fact that it could not be determined which of the sides fired a round. We can show you page 25 in this document, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure of the question and I don't know how this relates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's pull up the document and reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, this document has already been shown to the witness. I just wanted us to look at some of the pages that we showed to the previous witness, those that comprise UN conclusions. Can we look at page 25. Scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at bullet point 7: [In English] "It is not possible to state where the round was fired from ..." [Interpretation] Does this tally with your findings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Was that addressed at me, the question? Would you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this document we find several conclusions. For example, under bullet point 7 it is stated: [In English] "It is not possible to state where the round was fired from, as it could have been fired at any one of a number of different charges, giving a different range. It is certain that it was not hand-launched from a building ..." and so on. [Interpretation] With regard to the separation line and with regard to your conclusion that you could not determine where the round came from, would you say that bullet point 7 and the conclusion contained herein corresponds to your own conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I don't. I look at that particular comment, and my comment would agree with the finding of the board, which concluded the same thing as me, which was the minimum/maximum range straddled the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us also what prompted you to enter in your diary that perhaps -- that it was possible that one side actually shelled its own people? Was that ever mentioned before? Did that phenomena pervade the area, as it were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, it was just my own personal feeling. That's what I believed occurred in my own personal feeling, but in the report the facts did not prove that an individual side fired. For me it was minimum/maximum range across the confrontation line. Therefore, you could not specifically identify one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Thank you for having come to The Hague to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russell. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the next witness will be General Gauthier and he's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D05522 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, have you reviewed a hard copy of this statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Have I reviewed it? Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the copy?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect your words? Is this statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same ones that were put to you before you provided your statement, would your answers be the same today?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender the statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2368, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read a short summary of General Gauthier's statement in English. [In English] General Michel Gauthier joined the Canadian Armed Forces in 1973. He graduated from the Royal Military College in Kingston, Ontario, with a bachelor's degree in civil engineering. From September 1993 to August 1994, he was the UNPROFOR force engineer stationed at the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb. After his service in Bosnia, he rose in the ranks of the Canadian Armed Forces. At the time of his retirement from the Canadian Armed Forces in 2008 with the rank of lieutenant-general, he was the commander of all Canadian forces stationed abroad. After an explosion killed and wounded a large number of people in Markale -- at the Markale Market on the 5th of February, 1994, General Gauthier was assigned to a United Nations investigation into the incident. He was team leader. The team began their investigation on 11th of February, 1994. The team learned that the first crater analysis by the United Nations had been carried out by a team from French Battalion IV at approximately 14 hours on the day of the explosion. The FreBat -- French Battalion IV team had found a 120-millimetre mortar tail fin in the crater when they arrived on the scene. One of the French Battalion IV team members, Captain Segade, told him that in extracting the tail fin the analysis -- analysts had to chip away at the asphalt lip around the mouth of the crater and enlarge the actual hole formed by the penetration of the tail fin. In excavating the tail fin from the crater, the French Battalion IV team thereby disturbed the integrity of the crater for any analyses which followed. The French IV Battalion team did not measure the depth or angle of penetration of the tail fin nor did they calculate the angle of descent. The investigating team learned that Canadian Major John Russell, the military assistant to the deputy special representative of the Secretary-General, had conducted a crater analysis at approximately half past 16 hours on that -- on the day of explosion. It was reported that he had calculated the bearing of 450 mils and the angle of descent as between 2000 [sic] and 1300 mils. They interviewed Major Russell during their investigation and also obtained a copy of his report. When they arrived at the seen of the explosion on 11th of February, 1994, six days after the explosion, members of the investigating team examined the crater. They found that an accurate measurement of the direction of fire remained possible because the scrapes of the -- on the pavement remained untouched and the general location of a fuse tunnel could not have changed. Three members of the UN team independently calculated the direction of fire on 11th of February, 1994. Based upon the conditions -- condition of the crater, the investigative team was able to conclude that the direction of fire was between 330 and 420 mils from the point of detonation. Based upon the condition of the crater at the time of analysis by the team, they concluded that it was not possible to estimate the angle of descent with any acceptable degree of accuracy. They concluded that to ensure accuracy, the angle must be measured when the tail fin and fuse were -- fuse are in the ground. It was not done on February the 5th when the FrenchBat IV team excavated and removed the fin tail -- tail fin. Some members of the team made estimates of the angle of descent based upon the crater at the time of our investigation -- of their own investigation on the 11th of February, 1994. By the time the team conducted its crater analyses, six days had elapsed since the explosion. In the team's view, it was reasonable to suspect that the crater was thoroughly excavated by the local authorities during that period and the angles measured on 11th of February, 1994, were not beyond suspicion. The team's analysts believed that to assure accuracy, the angle must be measured when the tail fin and fuse are in the ground, and this was not done on 5th of February, 1994. It was assessed that the results measured on 11th of February, 1994, were not sufficiently accurate to be used as a basis for a finding based upon accepted crater analysis techniques. The investigating team concluded that the explosion on 5th of February, 1994, at the Markale Market in Sarajevo had been caused by a 120 mortar fired from a direction of 330 to 420 mils, and from a distance of between 300 and 5.551 metres. Since the distance of origin of fire overlapped each side of the confrontation line, they concluded that there was insufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or another fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb could have been fired by either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to put two other brief questions to you. Did your team ever dismiss the calculations made by Major Russell, the calculations that related to the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have I understood you correctly, you don't remember these calculations having been dismissed or rejected; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I cannot recall at this time our explicitly rejecting those calculations. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [In English] I pose it in English. Were you aware of any established method of crater analysis which allowed for calculation of the descent -- distance of mortar was fired from the depth of penetration of the tail fin?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, I don't have questions at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. As you have noted, General, your evidence in chief was admitted most in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be further

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And thank you for meeting with me yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one very small clarification, did you retire from the Canadian Armed Forces in 2008 [sic], as it appeared -- as was read out by Dr. Karadzic or 2009 as it appears in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now yesterday you told me that your first visit to Sarajevo was in March of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that predated your post as force engineer?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then as force engineer, you returned to Sarajevo many times thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to talk for a second about your responsibilities as force engineer. That included, I understand from you, planning and providing safe accommodation for UN troops and staff?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about mobility of UN across the mission area, did it include that as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: It most certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your responsibilities also included mine safety and clearance; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also told me yesterday that up until February 1994 you actually had little to no experience in crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Similarly, little to no experience in ballistics or blast effects?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct with respect to ballistics. With respect to blast effects, as a trained engineer and trained combat engineer, I have been trained in the use of explosives and calculation -- calculating the use of explosives to have a certain effect, for instance, to -- to block a road or to destroy a bridge and so on. So it's not quite correct to say I have no expertise in blast effects, but this is in the use of explosives for specific purposes and calculating the quantity and type of explosive to be used to achieve a certain effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. And up to that time, what you knew about mortars came largely from training exercises and in their use; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: That's correct. It was -- the training I'd had would have had more to do with the employment of mortars in support of military operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as a commander you've since had a great deal of experience in their use?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: To some degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would the degree of experience you've had allow you to confirm that mortars are generally used as area suppressing anti-personnel weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
